title: Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation for modulation of the inflammatory response after eccentric exercise
summary:
Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is currently receiving increased attention due to its potential effects on acute and chronic inflammation. Particularly in chronic diseases associated with systemic, low-grade inflammation, VNS offers a potentially promising, low side-effect approach to reducing this inflammation through various physiological mechanisms.
Physical exertion, particularly in sport, can trigger inflammatory processes depending on intensity and duration. Eccentric muscle stress in particular, in which the muscles are stretched during work (e.g. when running downhill), causes microtraumas in the muscles and leads to pronounced inflammatory reactions.
Against this background, the present experiment investigates to what extent a VNS can reduce or modulate inflammation induced by downhill running. In addition, we want to investigate whether and to what extent the metabolism and functionality of immune cells change under this influence. Furthermore, your subjective perception will be questioned at various times during the examination.

interventions.name: 45 minutes of downhill running (12% gradient) at 70% of VO2max followed by 3 hours of taVNS stimulation (Cymba Conchae)
45 minutes of downhill running (12% gradient) at 70% of VO2max followed by 3 hours of sham-stimulation (on the earlobe)
45 minutes of level running (1% slope) at 70% of VO2max without any stimulation

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
o Physically, neurologically and mentally healthy participants
o No intake of psychotropic medication
o Confirmed fitness for sport
Exclusion criteria:
o Acute/chronic psychiatric, immunological or neurological diseases
o More than 4 hours of endurance sport per week
o Regular intake of medication with psychotropic or immunological effects
o Smokers
o No confirmed fitness for sport at the first appointment
o Open wounds on the ear
o Skin diseases on the ear
o People with active implants (e.g. cochlear implant, pacemaker)
o People with cerebral shunt
